meta.title: way1ong Sky — a flight through the Solar System
meta.description: Fly between the Sun, the planets and the Moon — where they really are today. Free, no ads, no tracking.

app.name: Sky
app.scene: The Solar System in 3D. Drag to look around, pinch or scroll to come closer; pick a body from the list to fly to it.

scale.label: Scale
scale.handyNote: Handy scale: distances squeezed, bodies enlarged — everything fits one look. Directions are real.
scale.trueNote: True scale: sizes and distances as they are. The planets are specks in an emptiness — fly to one to see it.

status.noGraphics: This browser could not start 3D graphics, so the flight through the Solar System cannot be shown here; the map of the sky works.

time.label: Time
time.noSpin: At this speed the bodies’ spin about their own axes is not shown: it would only flicker. Their motion along the orbits is real.
time.limit: The app’s calendar ends here: it runs from {from} to {to}.

lunarAt.total: {date}: a total lunar eclipse. The whole Moon is in the Earth’s shadow. Time is stopped — let it run to watch the shadow leave.
lunarAt.partial: {date}: a partial lunar eclipse. Part of the Moon is in the Earth’s shadow. Time is stopped — let it run to watch the shadow move.

solarAt.total: {date}: a total solar eclipse. The dark spot on the Earth is the Moon’s shadow. Time is stopped — let it run to watch the spot cross the Earth.
solarAt.annular: {date}: an annular solar eclipse. The dim spot on the Earth is the Moon’s shadow; a ring of the Sun stays visible there. Time is stopped — let it run to watch the spot cross the Earth.
solarAt.partial: {date}: a partial solar eclipse. The dim patch on the Earth is the edge of the Moon’s shadow. Time is stopped — let it run to watch it move.

about.sun: The Sun is the star at the heart of our solar system, and the only star in it. It is a huge ball of hydrogen and helium held together by its own gravity, and it holds 99.8% of the solar system’s mass. Its gravity keeps everything in orbit, from the biggest planets to the smallest bits of debris.
about.mercury: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun and the smallest one, only slightly larger than the Earth’s Moon. Days there reach 430 °C; with no atmosphere to keep the heat, nights drop to −180 °C. It is the fastest planet: it goes around the Sun in 88 Earth days.
about.venus: Venus is the second planet from the Sun and the Earth’s closest planetary neighbor; in our sky it is the third brightest object after the Sun and the Moon. It is similar to the Earth in structure and size, but its thick atmosphere traps heat and makes it the hottest planet, with a surface hot enough to melt lead. Venus spins slowly, and in the opposite direction from most planets.
about.earth: The Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the biggest of the four planets closest to it, all made of rock and metal. It is the only place we know of inhabited by living things, and the only planet in the solar system with liquid water on its surface. Its atmosphere is 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 1% other gases, and it shields us from much of the Sun’s harmful radiation.
about.moon: The Moon is the Earth’s only natural satellite. It spins at the same rate as it goes around the Earth, so the same side always faces us; people first saw the far side in 1959, when a Soviet spacecraft flew past. Its surface is solid and rocky, cratered and pitted by impacts of asteroids, meteorites and comets.
about.mars: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun. It is called the Red Planet: iron minerals in its dirt oxidize, or rust, and make the surface look red. It is one of the most explored bodies in the solar system and the only planet where rovers have been sent; NASA missions have found lots of evidence that billions of years ago Mars was much wetter and warmer, with a thicker atmosphere.
about.jupiter: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the largest in the solar system — more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined. Its stripes and swirls are cold, windy clouds of ammonia and water in an atmosphere of hydrogen and helium. The Great Red Spot is a giant storm bigger than the Earth that has raged for hundreds of years.
about.saturn: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun and the second largest. Like Jupiter, it is a massive ball made mostly of hydrogen and helium. It is not the only planet with rings, but none are as spectacular or as complex as Saturn’s. It is the farthest planet from the Earth discovered by the unaided eye, known since ancient times.
about.uranus: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun and the third largest — a very cold and windy world. It rotates at a nearly 90-degree angle from the plane of its orbit, so it appears to spin sideways, rolling around the Sun like a ball. It was the first planet found with the aid of a telescope: the astronomer William Herschel discovered it in 1781.
about.neptune: Neptune is the eighth and most distant planet from the Sun, more than 30 times as far from it as the Earth. It is a dark, cold ice giant whipped by supersonic winds, and the only planet in our solar system not visible to the naked eye. It was discovered in 1846 and completed its first orbit around the Sun since then in 2011.

photo.sun: The Sun on 10 September 2025, taken by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory in extreme ultraviolet light. Our eyes cannot see this light; the gold colour is added.
photo.mercury: Mercury, seen by NASA’s MESSENGER spacecraft.
photo.venus: Venus, taken by NASA’s Mariner 10 spacecraft as it sped away from the planet; the picture was processed anew from the original data. The clouds in view are about 60 km above the surface.
photo.earth: The Earth, photographed by the Apollo 17 crew on 7 December 1972 on their way to the Moon. Almost the whole coastline of Africa is in view, with the Arabian Peninsula above and the south polar ice cap of Antarctica below.
photo.moon: The Moon, photographed on 6 April 2026 during NASA’s Artemis II mission. The near side, with its dark ancient lava flows, is the top half; the large crater below them is the Orientale basin, and everything below it is the far side.
photo.mars: Mars: a global colour view from Viking images.
photo.jupiter: Jupiter in true colour: four images taken by NASA’s Cassini spacecraft on 7 December 2000, projected onto a globe. The dark spot is the shadow of Jupiter’s moon Europa.
photo.saturn: Saturn and its rings in natural colour, taken by the Cassini spacecraft on 27 March 2004, on approach to the planet.
photo.uranus: Uranus, taken by the Voyager 2 spacecraft in 1986.
photo.neptune: Neptune, from the last whole-planet images of NASA’s Voyager 2, taken 4 days and 20 hours before its closest approach. The Great Dark Spot is in view.

keys: Arrow keys turn the view, plus and minus change the distance.

about.title: About
about.text: The bodies stand where they really are today; the positions are computed on your device. Nothing is sent anywhere: no ads, no tracking, no account.
about.textures: Maps of the Sun, the planets and the Moon, and the starry background: Solar System Scope, CC BY 4.0. The background is decoration: its stars are not placed by a catalogue.
about.facts: Sizes of the bodies and of Saturn’s rings: NASA fact sheets.
about.shadows: The Earth’s shadow on the Moon and the Moon’s on the Earth are computed from the real positions. The copper glow of the eclipsed Moon is a picture, not a measurement.
about.photos: Photos in the cards: NASA and its partners, named under each photo; some are cropped. This program is made independently of NASA.
about.sky: The sky from a place: stars — Wikidata (CC0); which stars are joined into constellations — d3-celestial by Olaf Frohn (BSD-3-Clause), after the charts of the IAU and Sky & Telescope; cities — Wikidata. Stars are drawn by day too, and the bending of light by the air near the horizon is not drawn. “Dark enough”, “in view” and “too faint for the eye” are the program’s own measures, not definitions of astronomy. For some stars Wikidata has no visual brightness: there the close Gaia G brightness is used. Proper names of stars: the names approved by the International Astronomical Union, from the list in Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0), and the titles of the stars’ articles in Wikipedia.

sites.title: Apollo landing places
sites.intro: Six Apollo missions landed people on the Moon between 1969 and 1972. Their landing places are also marked on the Moon itself when you look at it from near.

rows.orbit: Stayed in orbit around the Moon
rows.eva: Time outside on the surface, in all

photo.apollo11: An astronaut’s bootprint in the lunar soil, photographed during the Apollo 11 moonwalk on 20 July 1969.
photo.apollo12: Two NASA spacecraft on the Moon. In front is the uncrewed Surveyor 3, which landed on 19 April 1967; behind it, 600 feet (about 180 m) away, the Apollo 12 Lunar Module. Photographed on 20 November 1969.
photo.apollo14: The Apollo 14 Lunar Module with a circular flare from the brilliant Sun, photographed during the first moonwalk on 5 February 1971. At the far left is the lower slope of Cone Crater.
photo.apollo15: Hadley Rille, looking northwest, photographed during the first Apollo 15 moonwalk on 31 July 1971. Layers show in the wall of the rille, and blocks lie on its floor.
photo.apollo16: The Lunar Module “Orion” on the lunar surface, photographed by Charles M. Duke, Jr. during the first Apollo 16 moonwalk on 21 April 1972.
photo.apollo17: The Lunar Roving Vehicle that Eugene A. Cernan and Harrison H. Schmitt used extensively at the Taurus-Littrow landing place.

free.title: Free flight
free.note: Free flight: drag to look around; “Forward” and “Back” fly where you look — hold to keep flying. The nearer a body, the slower. To return, choose a body from the list.

sky.title: The sky: {place}
sky.scene: The sky over the chosen place: stars, constellations, the Sun, the Moon and the planets. Drag to look around.
sky.note: The sky over {place} at this moment. Drag to look around; two fingers or the wheel bring it nearer. The place is changed with the button below.
sky.dayNote: The Sun is up: the stars are drawn as if daylight did not hide them.

place.title: Place
place.intro: Choose the city whose sky you want to see. The program asks your phone nothing and sends nothing anywhere.
place.findLabel: Find a city or a country
place.none: No such city in the list. Choose the nearest large city: the sky over neighbouring cities is almost the same.

tonight.title: Tonight in the sky
tonight.place: {place}. Times are by the clock of your device.
tonight.darkNever: It does not get dark this night.
tonight.best: highest at {time}: {altitude}° over the horizon, to the {direction}
tonight.notSeen: not in view in the dark this night
tonight.shown: {name} at its highest this night: {date}. “Now” brings the present back.

install.title: On your phone or computer
install.text: The program can be installed like an app: it gets its own icon and opens without internet.
install.ios: On iPhone and iPad: tap “Share”, then “Add to Home Screen”. The program gets its own icon and opens without internet.
